policy.appliesTo: NEW dependencies — check-dependency, at add time
policy.description: Do not add a dependency if OSV reports known vulnerabilities for the target version. Prefer a fixed version or an alternative package.
policy.exceptions: Only proceed with a documented exception if no fixed version exists and risk is accepted by security.
policy.whyStricterThanThePlatform: Severity-blind rejection is deliberate here. Choosing a clean package at add time costs nothing, whereas the deployment platform's Trivy gate can only tell you afterwards that a CRITICAL is already in your image and blocking a release. Do not relax this to the platform's severity thresholds.

platformSeverityPolicy.appliesTo: EXISTING dependency trees — scan-dependencies, on a repo that already has a lockfile
platformSeverityPolicy.purpose: Speak the deployment platform's vocabulary, so a scan of what you already have is expressed in the same terms a promotion decision uses and can be prioritised accordingly. This is a SHARED VOCABULARY, not a prediction — see configurationIsNotVisible. It also does NOT replace the binary reject rule above for new dependencies.
platformSeverityPolicy.source: Deployment platform documentation — Trivy security scanning and production deployment (documented defaults)

decisions._source: documentedDefault — the platform's stated mapping, not a value we can read. Apply it to OUR findings for prioritisation; never assert it as the gate's outcome.

platformEnvKnobs._source: documentedDefault, NOT readable. These are platform-side environment variables; application users and internal teams cannot see their live values. Recorded so our report speaks the platform's language — never as a verified configuration.

configurationIsNotVisible.note: Trivy's scan parameters are platform-internal and are not shared with users or internal teams: we cannot read its flags, its ignore-file, which scanners are enabled, the check-bundle version, or the results bucket.
configurationIsNotVisible.divergesBothWays: A local OSV count can differ from the platform's in EITHER direction. The platform may suppress a finding we flag — an unfixed CVE under --ignore-unfixed, or an entry in an ignore-file we cannot see. It may also flag things we never scan at all (base-image OS packages, image layers, manifests, secrets). So a local CRITICAL does not prove a block, and a local all-clear does not prove a pass.
configurationIsNotVisible.reportingConsequence: Attribute every local verdict to THIS tool's policy, never to the platform's gate. Phrase it as 'our policy fails this' and 'the platform's documented default would classify it as X', never as 'the gate will block'. Get the live gate decision from the platform's own scan results or the platform team. Do not replace it with a local scan.

platformSeverityPolicy.severityFromOsv: OSV records carry severity in the 'severity' array (CVSS vectors) and in 'database_specific'/'ecosystem_specific' severity fields; osv-scanner also prints a severity column. Normalize to the five levels above. When no severity can be determined, treat it as UNKNOWN and say so — never silently assume LOW.
platformSeverityPolicy.coverageCaveat: OSV covers declared package dependencies only. The platform's Trivy also scans OS packages in the base image, the built image layers, IaC/Kubernetes manifests, and embedded secrets — a clean OSV scan does NOT predict a clean Trivy gate. State that when reporting.
platformSeverityPolicy.reportingRule: Group findings by decision (block / approval_required / warn / informational) as the platform's DOCUMENTED DEFAULT applied to our findings. Never present an OSV result as the platform's verdict. Point the reader at the platform's own scan results or the platform team for the actual state.

scanner.scanBunLock: node plugins/scan-dependency/scripts/scan-lockfile.js . — bun.lock packages are queried through the OSV batch API (endpoints.querybatch, then endpoints.vuln per id) whether or not osv-scanner is installed; osv-scanner's own bun.lock support is not relied on.
